meta.note: Original CISSP-style practice questions. matching questions carry a prompts[] (left items numbered 1..n) and options[] (right items A..n); correct_answer encodes the pairing. sequence_ordering correct_answer lists option labels in correct order.

questions.question: A network switch primarily forwards frames to the correct port based on:

explanation.why_correct: A switch operates at Layer 2, directing frames to the appropriate port based on destination MAC address (multilayer switches can also do Layer 3).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Routing by IP subnet is a Layer 3 router function (though multilayer switches can also route).
why_others_are_wrong.D: Port-number filtering is a transport/application-layer firewall function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Cable color is irrelevant to switching decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps MAC-based frame forwarding to a Layer 2 switch.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: A router operates primarily at which OSI layer to forward packets between networks?

explanation.why_correct: A router operates at Layer 3, using a route table/policies to forward packets between different networks based on IP addresses.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Layer 1 devices (repeaters/hubs) deal with raw bits/signals.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Layer 2 devices (switches/bridges) forward by MAC address.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Layer 7 is the application layer, not routing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps IP packet forwarding to a Layer 3 router.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Why is a switch generally more secure and efficient than a hub?

options.label: A
options.text: A switch encrypts all traffic while a hub does not

options.label: B
options.text: A hub performs deep packet inspection

options.label: C
options.text: A switch forwards frames only to the destination port, while a hub repeats traffic to all ports

options.label: D
options.text: A hub operates at Layer 3 while a switch operates at Layer 1

explanation.why_correct: A switch directs frames only to the intended port (reducing exposure and collisions), whereas a hub repeats incoming signals out all ports.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Neither device encrypts traffic by default.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A hub is a Layer 1 device and a switch is Layer 2 (this is reversed).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Deep packet inspection is an NGFW capability, not a hub function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Contrasts selective switch forwarding with hub flooding.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Which device connects network segments that use DIFFERENT protocols, translating between them?

explanation.why_correct: A gateway connects networks using different protocols, performing translation between them.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A repeater regenerates signals on the same medium (Layer 1).
why_others_are_wrong.B: A hub repeats signals to all ports (Layer 1).
why_others_are_wrong.D: A bridge connects two segments using the SAME protocol (Layer 2).

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps protocol translation to a gateway.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: A "brouter" is best described as a device that:

options.label: A
options.text: Only repeats electrical signals at Layer 1

options.label: B
options.text: Combines bridge and router functions—routing at Layer 3 when possible, otherwise bridging at Layer 2

options.label: C
options.text: Assigns IP addresses dynamically to hosts

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypts all traffic at the application layer

explanation.why_correct: A brouter combines a bridge and a router, routing using Layer 3 when possible and defaulting to Layer 2 bridging otherwise.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Signal repetition at Layer 1 describes a repeater.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Application-layer encryption is unrelated to a brouter.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Dynamic IP assignment is DHCP's function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the brouter's combined bridge/router behavior.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: A repeater is a Layer 1 device whose primary purpose is to:

options.label: C
options.text: Regenerate and extend a signal to overcome distance/attenuation

explanation.why_correct: A repeater regenerates/amplifies signals at the physical layer to extend transmission distance.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Routing between subnets is a Layer 3 router function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Application-content filtering is an application-layer proxy/NGFW function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Protocol translation is a gateway function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps signal regeneration to a Layer 1 repeater.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Match each network device (1-4) to the OSI layer at which it primarily operates (A-D).

explanation.why_correct: Hub/Repeater → Layer 1 (B); Switch/Bridge → Layer 2 (A); Router → Layer 3 (D); Application-level proxy → Layer 7 (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of devices to their OSI layers.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: A proxy that makes requests to the internet on behalf of internal clients primarily helps security by:

options.label: D
options.text: Hiding internal client details and allowing inspection/filtering of requests

explanation.why_correct: A proxy acts as an intermediary, concealing internal hosts and enabling content inspection/filtering of outbound/inbound requests.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Proxies do not exist to enlarge broadcast domains.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Data-at-rest encryption is unrelated to a forwarding proxy.
why_others_are_wrong.B: MAC assignment is not a proxy function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the intermediary/concealment role of a proxy.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Which UPS type continuously powers equipment from its battery/inverter, providing the cleanest, most consistent power with no transfer time?

explanation.why_correct: An online/double-conversion UPS always powers the load through the battery/inverter, delivering consistent, clean power with effectively no transfer delay.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A standby/offline UPS only switches to battery when power fails, with a brief transfer time.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A line-interactive UPS adds automatic voltage regulation but is not full double-conversion.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A generator provides long-term backup power but is not a UPS and has startup delay.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes online (double-conversion) from standby and line-interactive UPS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Infrastructure Operations

questions.question: A line-interactive UPS adds which capability over a basic standby UPS?

options.label: A
options.text: Automatic Voltage Regulation (AVR) to stabilize power fluctuations

explanation.why_correct: A line-interactive UPS includes AVR to stabilize voltage fluctuations (sags/surges) without switching to battery.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Routing is a router function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Deep packet inspection is an NGFW feature.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless access is a WAP function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps AVR to the line-interactive UPS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Infrastructure Operations

questions.question: A data center needs to maintain operations through a multi-hour utility outage. Beyond a UPS, what provides the LONG-TERM backup power, and what does it require?

options.label: A
options.text: A generator, which requires a steady fuel supply and regular maintenance

options.label: B
options.text: A proxy server, which requires more bandwidth

options.label: C
options.text: A larger broadcast domain, which requires more switches

options.label: D
options.text: A line-interactive UPS alone, which needs no fuel

explanation.why_correct: A generator provides long-term backup power for extended outages but requires a steady fuel supply and regular maintenance/testing; the UPS bridges the gap until the generator starts.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Broadcast domains are unrelated to power continuity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A UPS provides only short-duration power and cannot sustain multi-hour outages.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A proxy is a network-traffic intermediary, not a power source.

questions.exam_reasoning: Pairs long-term outage coverage with generators (UPS bridges short term).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Infrastructure Operations

questions.question: When a vendor announces End of Service (EOS) for a network appliance, it means:

options.label: A
options.text: The product gains new premium features

options.label: B
options.text: The product's warranty is automatically extended indefinitely

options.label: C
options.text: The vendor will no longer provide support and updates for the product

explanation.why_correct: End of Service/Support means the vendor terminates support and updates; running such gear risks unpatched vulnerabilities and should be planned for replacement.

why_others_are_wrong.D: The device may still run; the risk is lack of support/patches.
why_others_are_wrong.A: EOS removes support; it does not add features.
why_others_are_wrong.B: EOS typically coincides with the end of warranty/support, not extension.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of EOS as the end of vendor support/updates.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Infrastructure Operations

questions.question: A key SECURITY advantage of fiber-optic cabling over copper twisted pair is that fiber:

options.label: A
options.text: Requires no physical protection at all

options.label: B
options.text: Does not emit electromagnetic signals that can be tapped via emanations and resists EMI

options.label: C
options.text: Is always cheaper and easier to install

options.label: D
options.text: Automatically encrypts the data it carries

explanation.why_correct: Fiber transmits light through a glass core, producing no electromagnetic emanations to intercept and being immune to EMI—harder to tap passively than copper.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Fiber is typically more expensive and harder to terminate than copper.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Fiber does not encrypt data; it is just a medium.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Fiber still requires physical protection from damage and intrusion.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests fiber's emanation/EMI security advantage.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Fiber Optic Cabling

questions.question: Cabling must be run through a building's air-handling (plenum) spaces above the ceiling. Which cable property is MOST important for safety here?

options.label: A
options.text: Plenum-rated cabling that emits less toxic smoke when burning

options.label: B
options.text: The lowest-cost cable regardless of fire rating

options.label: C
options.text: A cable with the highest possible bandwidth only

explanation.why_correct: Plenum spaces circulate air; plenum-rated cable uses fire-resistant jacketing that emits less toxic smoke if it burns, a life-safety requirement.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Jacket color does not affect fire safety in plenum spaces.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Using non-plenum cable in plenum spaces violates fire codes and endangers life.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Bandwidth alone does not address the plenum fire-safety requirement.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests plenum-rated cable selection for air-handling spaces.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Fiber Optic Cabling

questions.question: Shielded Twisted Pair (STP) is preferable to Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) primarily in environments with:

explanation.why_correct: STP adds shielding to reduce the effects of EMI/crosstalk, making it preferable in electrically noisy environments; UTP is cheaper where EMI is low.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Cabling choice is unrelated to the absence of power.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Wireless devices do not use twisted-pair cabling.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fiber endpoints would use fiber, not twisted pair.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps EMI environments to the value of STP shielding.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Twisted Pair Cables

questions.question: Which network topology provides the HIGHEST redundancy because every node connects to every other node?

explanation.why_correct: A (full) mesh topology connects every node to every other node, maximizing redundancy and fault tolerance at higher cost.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A bus topology shares a single backbone—a single break can disrupt the segment.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A star topology depends on a central device whose failure affects all nodes.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A single link offers no redundancy.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps full interconnection/redundancy to mesh topology.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Transmission Media - Part 1

questions.question: In a star topology where all hosts connect to a single central switch, what is the PRIMARY availability concern?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot support more than two devices

options.label: B
options.text: Every host can read every other host's traffic by default

options.label: C
options.text: The central device is a single point of failure for the whole segment

options.label: D
options.text: Adding a new host requires rewiring all existing hosts

explanation.why_correct: In a star topology, all nodes depend on the central device; its failure takes down the entire segment, making it a single point of failure.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A switch (unlike a hub) does not flood all traffic to every host by default.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Adding a host only requires connecting it to the central device, not rewiring others.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A star can support many devices, limited by the central device's capacity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the single-point-of-failure risk of star topology.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Transmission Media - Part 1

questions.question: A network connecting devices across a large geographic area, such as between cities or countries, is a:

explanation.why_correct: A WAN spans large geographic areas (e.g., between cities/countries), often using carrier links.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A LAN covers a small area like a single building or campus.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A PAN covers a very short range around a person (e.g., Bluetooth).
why_others_are_wrong.C: A MAN spans a city/metropolitan area—larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes WAN from LAN/MAN/PAN by scope.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Types

questions.question: Bluetooth connecting a phone to nearby wireless earbuds is an example of a:

explanation.why_correct: A PAN is a very short-range network around an individual, commonly using Bluetooth.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A WAN spans large geographic distances.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A MAN spans a metropolitan area.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A SAN is a specialized storage network, not a personal Bluetooth link.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps short-range Bluetooth to a PAN.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Types

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes baseband from broadband transmission?

options.label: A
options.text: Baseband uses the entire medium for a single channel; broadband divides the medium into multiple channels

options.label: B
options.text: Broadband can carry only one signal at a time

options.label: C
options.text: Baseband always uses fiber; broadband always uses copper

options.label: D
options.text: Baseband is wireless and broadband is wired

explanation.why_correct: Baseband dedicates the whole medium to one signal/channel at a time, while broadband splits the medium into multiple simultaneous channels/frequencies.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Neither is tied to a specific cable type by definition.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Broadband carries multiple signals simultaneously, not just one.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Both can be wired; the distinction is single vs. multiple channels.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the single-channel vs multi-channel distinction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Types of Communications

questions.question: A communication method that allows both parties to send and receive data SIMULTANEOUSLY is:

explanation.why_correct: Full duplex permits simultaneous two-way communication; half duplex allows two-way but only one direction at a time; simplex is one-way only.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Half duplex allows only one direction at a time.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Simplex is strictly one-way.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Baseband refers to channel usage, not directionality.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes full duplex from half duplex and simplex.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Communication Methods

questions.question: Which protocol is widely used to monitor and manage the status of network devices (e.g., routers, switches)?

explanation.why_correct: SNMP is used to monitor and manage network devices, collecting status and performance data (use SNMPv3 for security).

why_others_are_wrong.A: SMTP routes email.
why_others_are_wrong.D: ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses.
why_others_are_wrong.B: FTP transfers files.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps device monitoring/management to SNMP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Monitoring Protocols

questions.question: Which protocol is used by the ping and traceroute utilities to report communication status, and has no assigned port?

explanation.why_correct: ICMP provides communication status and error messages and underlies ping and traceroute; it has no port number.

why_others_are_wrong.B: SNMP manages devices and uses ports 161/162.
why_others_are_wrong.A: HTTP serves web content on port 80.
why_others_are_wrong.C: DHCP assigns IP addresses on ports 67/68.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps ping/traceroute to ICMP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Monitoring Protocols

questions.question: Order the network monitoring process steps as described in the guide. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The monitoring process flows from collecting data, to monitoring it, to detecting anomalies, to taking action.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered network-monitoring process.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Process of Network Monitoring

questions.question: A primary security-related purpose of network monitoring is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Observe network performance and detect anomalies that may indicate a security issue

options.label: B
options.text: Permanently prevent any device from ever failing

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the need for firewalls entirely

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt all data at rest automatically

explanation.why_correct: Network monitoring focuses on performance and visibility, enabling detection of anomalies that can indicate attacks or failures.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Monitoring detects issues; it cannot prevent all hardware failures.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Monitoring does not perform data-at-rest encryption.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Monitoring complements, not replaces, firewalls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties monitoring to visibility and anomaly detection.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Purposes of Network Monitoring

questions.question: Which TWO devices make forwarding decisions using Layer 2 (MAC) information? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Bridges and switches are Layer 2 devices that forward based on MAC addresses.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A router forwards at Layer 3 using IP addresses.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A repeater operates at Layer 1, regenerating signals without MAC decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the Layer 2 forwarding devices.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Which TWO measures improve the AVAILABILITY of network infrastructure during power problems? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Using a hub instead of a switch

explanation.why_correct: UPS units cover short outages/fluctuations and generators sustain long outages—both improve availability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling monitoring reduces visibility and does not aid power availability.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Replacing a switch with a hub harms performance/security and is unrelated to power.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies power-availability measures.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Network Infrastructure Operations

questions.question: Coaxial cable carries signals over which medium?

options.label: A
options.text: A copper core surrounded by shielding

explanation.why_correct: Coaxial cable uses a central copper conductor surrounded by insulation and metallic shielding to carry electrical signals.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A glass core using light describes fiber optic cable.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Open-air radio waves describe wireless transmission.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Bundled fiber strands describe fiber cabling, not coax.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of coaxial cable construction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Coaxial Cable

questions.question: A Wireless Access Point (WAP) primarily:

options.label: A
options.text: Routes packets between autonomous systems on the internet

options.label: B
options.text: Generates backup power for the data center

options.label: D
options.text: Bridges wireless client devices onto a wired network

explanation.why_correct: A WAP connects wireless clients to a wired LAN, acting as a bridge between the wireless and wired segments.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Inter-AS routing on the internet is a BGP/router function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup power is a generator/UPS function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Media sanitization is a data-destruction activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps wireless-to-wired bridging to a WAP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Components > Hardware Operations

questions.question: Wireless networks use CSMA/CA rather than CSMA/CD primarily because:

options.label: A
options.text: Wireless media never experience any contention

options.label: B
options.text: Stations cannot reliably detect collisions on wireless media, so they try to AVOID them

options.label: C
options.text: Collision detection is illegal on wireless networks

explanation.why_correct: On shared wireless media, a transmitting station cannot reliably hear collisions (hidden-node problem), so CSMA/CA focuses on avoidance rather than detection (CSMA/CD, used on wired Ethernet).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Wireless media do experience contention; that is why a MAC method is needed.
why_others_are_wrong.C: There is no legal prohibition; it is a technical limitation.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CSMA/CA is a media-access method, not an encryption scheme.

questions.exam_reasoning: Explains why wireless uses collision avoidance (CA) vs detection (CD).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Collision Management

questions.question: Routing and logical addressing for packet delivery between networks occur at which OSI layer?

explanation.why_correct: Layer 3 (Network) manages routing and logical (IP) addressing for packet transfer between networks.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Layer 2 handles MAC addressing and frames within a segment.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Layer 4 manages end-to-end logical connections (TCP/UDP).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Layer 7 provides the application interface.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps routing/logical addressing to Layer 3.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > OSI Model Layers

questions.question: The OSI Transport layer (Layer 4) is responsible for:

options.label: B
options.text: Controlling logical end-to-end connections (e.g., TCP connection-oriented, UDP connectionless)

options.label: C
options.text: Resolving IP addresses to MAC addresses

options.label: D
options.text: Converting frames into bits for the physical medium

explanation.why_correct: Layer 4 controls end-to-end logical connections—TCP (connection-oriented) and UDP (connectionless).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Bit conversion for the medium is Layer 1 (Physical).
why_others_are_wrong.C: IP-to-MAC resolution (ARP) is a Layer 2/3 function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The user interface is Layer 7 (Application).

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps end-to-end TCP/UDP connections to Layer 4.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > OSI Model Layers

questions.question: At the OSI Network layer, the protocol data unit (PDU) is called a:

explanation.why_correct: The Network layer PDU is the packet; Transport = segment, Data Link = frame, Physical = bits.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A segment is the Transport-layer PDU.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A frame is the Data Link-layer PDU.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Bits are the Physical-layer PDU.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the Network-layer PDU.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Protocol Data Unit (PDU)

questions.question: Match each OSI layer (1-4) to its protocol data unit (A-D).

explanation.why_correct: Transport → Segment (B); Network → Packet (A); Data Link → Frame (D); Physical → Bits (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of layers to their PDUs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Protocol Data Unit (PDU)

questions.question: During encapsulation, data is wrapped as it moves DOWN the stack from the sending application to the wire. Order the PDUs from first formed to last. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: Encapsulation proceeds Data → Segment → Packet → Frame (then bits on the wire) as each lower layer adds its header.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the encapsulation order down the stack.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Encapsulation Process

questions.question: Order the messages of the TCP three-way handshake. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The TCP handshake is SYN (client initiates), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and responds), ACK (client confirms), after which data transfer begins.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the TCP handshake sequence.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > TCP Three-Way Handshake

questions.question: A live video-conferencing application prioritizes low latency and can tolerate occasional lost frames. Which transport protocol is the BETTER fit, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: TCP, because guaranteed delivery is essential for real-time video

options.label: B
options.text: UDP, because it is connectionless and avoids handshake/retransmission overhead

options.label: C
options.text: ICMP, because it carries the video payload efficiently

options.label: D
options.text: ARP, because it resolves addresses quickly

explanation.why_correct: UDP is connectionless and lightweight (no handshake/retransmission), favoring low-latency real-time media that tolerates minor loss; TCP's reliability adds latency.

why_others_are_wrong.A: TCP's retransmission/ordering adds latency that harms real-time media.
why_others_are_wrong.D: ARP resolves IP-to-MAC; it does not carry application data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ICMP carries control/status messages, not video payloads.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests choosing UDP for latency-sensitive media.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Layer 4 - Transport Layer Protocols

questions.question: Which transport protocol is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery using a handshake?

explanation.why_correct: TCP is connection-oriented, establishing a session via the three-way handshake and providing reliable, ordered delivery.

why_others_are_wrong.A: UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IP is a connectionless Layer 3 routing protocol.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ICMP carries status/error messages, not reliable data streams.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps reliable, connection-oriented delivery to TCP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Layer 4 - Transport Layer Protocols

questions.question: Which of the following is a private (RFC 1918) IPv4 address range?

why_others_are_wrong.B: 8.0.0.0/8 is public address space.
why_others_are_wrong.C: 1.0.0.0/8 is public address space.
why_others_are_wrong.A: 224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255 is Class D multicast, not private unicast.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the 10.0.0.0/8 private range.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > IPv4 Private Address Ranges (RFC 1918)

questions.question: Network Address Translation (NAT) primarily enables:

options.label: A
options.text: Encryption of all packets leaving the network

options.label: B
options.text: Private internal IP addresses to be translated to public addresses for internet routing

options.label: C
options.text: Resolution of domain names to IP addresses

explanation.why_correct: NAT translates private (RFC 1918) addresses to public addresses (and back) so internal hosts can communicate over the internet; PAT maps many hosts to one public IP via ports.

why_others_are_wrong.A: NAT does not encrypt traffic.
why_others_are_wrong.D: MAC assignment is done by hardware, not NAT.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Name-to-IP resolution is DNS's job.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps private-to-public translation to NAT.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > IPv4 Private Address Ranges (RFC 1918)

questions.question: A small office has 50 internal hosts but only one public IP address from its ISP, and all hosts need internet access. Which technique makes this possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Port Address Translation (PAT), mapping many private hosts to one public IP using unique ports

options.label: C
options.text: Assigning each host a Class A public block

options.label: D
options.text: Using DNSSEC to share the address

explanation.why_correct: PAT (NAT overload) maps many internal hosts to a single public IP by tracking unique source ports per connection.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A single ISP-assigned public IP cannot provide a public block per host.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling NAT would leave private hosts unable to route to the internet.
why_others_are_wrong.D: DNSSEC authenticates DNS responses; it does not share an IP among hosts.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps many-to-one public IP sharing to PAT.

questions.question: The CIDR notation /24 corresponds to which subnet mask?

explanation.why_correct: /24 means 24 network bits, i.e., the mask 255.255.255.0 (the traditional Class C default).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > CIDR Notation for Subnet Masks

questions.question: IPv4 addresses in the range 224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255 (Class D) are reserved for:

explanation.why_correct: Class D (224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255) is reserved for multicast.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Private addressing uses RFC 1918 ranges in Classes A/B/C.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Loopback is 127.0.0.0/8.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Experimental use is Class E (240.0.0.0+).

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps Class D to multicast.

questions.question: A benefit of IPv6 over IPv4 highlighted in the guide is that IPv6:

options.label: C
options.text: Has a vast address space and built-in autoconfiguration that reduces the need for NAT

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminates the need for any routing

explanation.why_correct: IPv6 provides an enormous address space and built-in configuration (reducing reliance on NAT/DHCP), plus features like scoped addresses and QoS.

why_others_are_wrong.A: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, longer than IPv4's 32-bit.
why_others_are_wrong.B: IPv6 supports QoS for traffic prioritization.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IPv6 still relies on routing between networks.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests IPv6 address-space/autoconfiguration benefits.

questions.question: Which TWO address ranges are RFC 1918 private ranges? (Select TWO.)

why_others_are_wrong.C: 11.0.0.0/8 is public address space (only 10.0.0.0/8 is private in Class A).
why_others_are_wrong.A: 200.1.x is public address space.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the 172.16/12 and 192.168/16 private ranges.

questions.question: Which statement about broadcast and collision domains is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A hub separates both collision and broadcast domains per port

options.label: B
options.text: Switches and hubs are functionally identical for collision domains

options.label: C
options.text: A router places all connected networks in one broadcast domain

options.label: D
options.text: A switch separates collision domains per port, while a router separates broadcast domains

explanation.why_correct: Each switch port is its own collision domain; routers bound broadcast domains (broadcasts do not cross a router by default).

why_others_are_wrong.A: A hub is a single shared collision domain (no separation per port).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Routers separate broadcast domains rather than merging them.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A hub is one collision domain; a switch gives each port its own—so they differ.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests how switches and routers bound collision/broadcast domains.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Network Domains

questions.question: A dynamic route differs from a static route in that a dynamic route is:

options.label: C
options.text: Automatically learned and updated by routing protocols exchanging information with neighbors

options.label: D
options.text: Always more secure than any static route

explanation.why_correct: Dynamic routes are learned/updated automatically via routing protocols that share information with neighboring routers, adapting to topology changes.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Manual, unchanging configuration describes a static route.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Dynamic routing is not inherently more secure; it can introduce protocol risks.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Dynamic routing is used on wired and wireless networks alike.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes dynamic (learned) from static (manual) routes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Types of Routes

questions.question: A link-state routing protocol differs from a distance-vector protocol in that link-state protocols:

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot operate within an autonomous system

options.label: B
options.text: Build a map of the overall network state to select the most reliable/fastest routes

options.label: C
options.text: Choose paths based only on hop count and direction

options.label: D
options.text: Never converge after a topology change

explanation.why_correct: Link-state protocols compute routes from a complete view of network topology/state (e.g., OSPF), often yielding faster, more reliable paths than hop-count-based distance-vector protocols.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Choosing by hop count/direction describes distance-vector protocols (e.g., RIP).
why_others_are_wrong.A: Link-state protocols (like OSPF) commonly run as interior gateway protocols within an AS.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Link-state protocols do converge; they are often faster to converge than distance-vector.

questions.exam_reasoning: Contrasts link-state topology awareness with distance-vector hop counting.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Routing Protocol Types

questions.question: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is used to exchange routing information:

options.label: A
options.text: Between different autonomous systems (as an exterior gateway protocol)

options.label: B
options.text: Between USB devices on a host

options.label: C
options.text: To assign IP addresses to clients

explanation.why_correct: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol used to exchange routing information between autonomous systems (e.g., across the internet).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Switch-internal forwarding is not BGP's role.
why_others_are_wrong.B: USB device communication is unrelated to routing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: IP assignment is DHCP's function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps inter-AS routing to BGP/EGP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Types of Routing Protocols

questions.question: Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) such as OSPF are used to exchange routing information:

options.label: A
options.text: Only between competing internet service providers

options.label: B
options.text: To translate private IPs to public IPs

explanation.why_correct: IGPs (e.g., OSPF, EIGRP, RIP) exchange routing data within a single autonomous system; EGPs (e.g., BGP) operate between autonomous systems.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Routing between different systems/ISPs is the role of EGPs like BGP.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IGPs are not limited to Bluetooth and typically run over wired/enterprise links.
why_others_are_wrong.B: IP translation is NAT, not a routing protocol.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps intra-AS routing to IGPs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Types of Routing Protocols

questions.question: An Autonomous System (AS) is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A single laptop with no network connection

options.label: B
options.text: A type of fire suppression system

options.label: D
options.text: A collection of network devices managed under a single routing policy

explanation.why_correct: An AS is a set of networks/devices under a common administration and routing policy, identified by an AS number for inter-AS routing.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A standalone laptop is not an AS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control, unrelated to routing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless encryption (e.g., WPA2) is not an AS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the autonomous system concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Types of Routing Protocols

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts a MAC address with an IP address?

options.label: A
options.text: A MAC address is logical and an IP address is physical

options.label: B
options.text: Both are assigned by DHCP at boot time

options.label: D
options.text: A MAC address is a physical Layer 2 hardware address; an IP address is a logical Layer 3 address

explanation.why_correct: A MAC address is a hardware (physical) address used at Layer 2; an IP address is a logical Layer 3 address that can change (e.g., via DHCP).

why_others_are_wrong.A: This reverses the definitions—MAC is physical, IP is logical.
why_others_are_wrong.B: MAC addresses are burned into hardware, not assigned by DHCP (which assigns IPs).
why_others_are_wrong.C: They operate at Layers 2 and 3, not Layer 7.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes physical MAC from logical IP addressing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > IP Networking

questions.question: Which TWO are distance-vector routing protocols? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: RIP and BGP are categorized as distance-vector (BGP is a path-vector variant) in the guide; OSPF is link-state and TLS is not a routing protocol.

why_others_are_wrong.C: OSPF is a link-state protocol.
why_others_are_wrong.B: TLS is a transport-layer security protocol, not a routing protocol.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies distance-vector protocols versus link-state and non-routing protocols.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Key Routing Protocols

questions.question: MAC addressing and frame delivery within a local segment occur at which OSI layer?

explanation.why_correct: Layer 2 (Data Link) handles hardware (MAC) addressing and frame delivery within a network segment.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Layer 3 handles logical IP addressing and routing between networks.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Layer 4 handles end-to-end transport (TCP/UDP).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Layer 5 manages sessions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps MAC/frame delivery to Layer 2.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > OSI Model Layers

questions.question: Establishing, maintaining, and terminating communication sessions between applications is the role of which OSI layer?

explanation.why_correct: Layer 5 (Session) establishes, maintains, and terminates sessions between communicating systems.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Layer 1 transmits raw bits.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Layer 3 routes packets.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Layer 2 delivers frames within a segment.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps session management to Layer 5.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > OSI Model Layers

questions.question: A Class A IPv4 network has which default subnet mask?

explanation.why_correct: Class A uses a default /8 mask (255.0.0.0), providing a large number of hosts per network.

why_others_are_wrong.C: /16 (255.255.0.0) is the Class B default.
why_others_are_wrong.B: /24 (255.255.255.0) is the Class C default.
why_others_are_wrong.A: /32 denotes a single host, not a class default.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps Class A to the /8 default mask.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > IPv4 Classes

questions.question: The four-layer TCP/IP model consists of the Application, Transport, Internet, and ________ layers.

explanation.why_correct: The TCP/IP model has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, and Link (Network Access).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Session is an OSI layer, not a separate TCP/IP model layer.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Presentation is an OSI layer, folded into Application in TCP/IP.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Data Center" is not a TCP/IP model layer.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the four TCP/IP model layers.

questions.question: iSCSI is an example of a converged protocol because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Merges the SCSI storage protocol with IP networking to allow remote storage access

options.label: B
options.text: Replaces the need for any cabling

options.label: C
options.text: Routes traffic only within a single VLAN

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypts all wireless traffic using AES

explanation.why_correct: iSCSI converges the SCSI storage command protocol with TCP/IP networking, enabling block storage access over standard IP networks.

why_others_are_wrong.D: AES wireless encryption (WPA2/3) is unrelated to iSCSI.
why_others_are_wrong.B: iSCSI runs over IP networks, which require cabling/infrastructure.
why_others_are_wrong.C: iSCSI is not limited to a single VLAN.

questions.question: An attacker hides data exfiltration inside the unused fields and timing of an otherwise legitimate protocol so it blends with normal traffic. This abuse of encapsulation is known as:

explanation.why_correct: Covert channels (storage- or timing-based) abuse encapsulation/protocol features to hide unauthorized communication within legitimate-looking traffic, often bypassing detection.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A broadcast storm is excessive broadcast traffic, not hidden exfiltration.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A three-way handshake establishes a TCP connection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A default route is a routing configuration, not a hidden channel.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps hidden protocol-based exfiltration to covert channels.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Multilayer Protocols

questions.question: The IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 is commonly used as the:

options.label: C
options.text: Loopback (localhost) address for testing the local TCP/IP stack

explanation.why_correct: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback/localhost address used to test the local TCP/IP stack on the host itself.

why_others_are_wrong.D: The default gateway is a router interface address, not loopback.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A broadcast address is the highest address in a subnet, not 127.0.0.1.
why_others_are_wrong.A: 127.0.0.1 is internal to the host, not a public DNS server.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the loopback address.

questions.question: During encapsulation, what happens to data as it moves down the OSI stack?

options.label: A
options.text: Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) information

options.label: B
options.text: Each layer removes a header to expose the payload

options.label: C
options.text: The data is converted to a single packet with no changes

options.label: D
options.text: The data is encrypted at every layer automatically

explanation.why_correct: Encapsulation adds headers (and trailers) at each descending layer, forming segments, packets, frames, and finally bits; the reverse (de-encapsulation) strips them on receipt.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Removing headers is de-encapsulation, which occurs on the receiving side moving up the stack.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Encapsulation itself does not automatically encrypt at every layer.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The data changes form (segment/packet/frame/bits) as headers are added.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the header-adding nature of encapsulation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Encapsulation Process

questions.question: Which protocol should REPLACE Telnet for remote command-line administration because it encrypts the session?

explanation.why_correct: SSH provides encrypted remote access and should replace Telnet, which transmits credentials and commands in cleartext.

why_others_are_wrong.A: HTTP is for unencrypted web traffic, not remote shell access.
why_others_are_wrong.D: SNMPv1 monitors devices and is itself insecure; it is not a remote shell.
why_others_are_wrong.B: FTP transfers files in cleartext and is not a secure remote shell.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps secure remote administration to SSH over Telnet.

questions.question: HTTPS provides secure web communication primarily by using:

options.label: D
options.text: TLS (formerly SSL) to encrypt the session

explanation.why_correct: HTTPS secures web traffic by layering HTTP over TLS (which replaced SSL), providing confidentiality and integrity.

why_others_are_wrong.A: ARP resolves IP-to-MAC addresses; it does not encrypt web traffic.
why_others_are_wrong.B: NAT translates addresses; it does not provide encryption.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ICMP carries status/error messages, not web encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps HTTPS security to TLS.

questions.question: A security review finds employees logging into a device management interface over Telnet across the corporate LAN. What is the PRIMARY risk and best remediation?

options.label: A
options.text: Credentials travel in cleartext and can be sniffed; replace Telnet with SSH

options.label: B
options.text: Telnet encrypts too strongly; downgrade to HTTP

options.label: C
options.text: Telnet uses too much bandwidth; switch to UDP

options.label: D
options.text: There is no risk because it is on the internal LAN

explanation.why_correct: Telnet sends credentials and commands in cleartext, exposing them to sniffing (including internal threats); SSH provides an encrypted replacement.

why_others_are_wrong.C: The risk is confidentiality (cleartext), not bandwidth.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Telnet does not encrypt at all; HTTP is also cleartext.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Internal networks are not inherently trusted (insider/lateral-movement risk).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognizing cleartext-protocol exposure and the SSH remediation.

questions.question: DNP3 is a protocol most commonly associated with:

options.label: D
options.text: Industrial control systems (e.g., electric, water, oil and gas)

explanation.why_correct: DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol v3) is widely used in industrial control systems such as electric utilities, water/wastewater, and oil and gas.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Email encryption uses S/MIME or PGP, not DNP3.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Name resolution is DNS.
why_others_are_wrong.A: IP assignment is DHCP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps DNP3 to ICS environments.

questions.question: How does a stateful inspection firewall improve on a static (stateless) packet-filtering firewall?

options.label: A
options.text: It only inspects the source IP and nothing else

options.label: D
options.text: It tracks the state of active connections to decide which packets belong to a legitimate session

explanation.why_correct: A stateful firewall maintains a state table of active connections (Layers 3-4), allowing return traffic that belongs to established sessions and blocking unsolicited packets.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Inspecting only source IP describes basic stateless filtering.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Stateful inspection works at Layers 3-4, not Layer 1.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Stateful firewalls do block traffic based on policy and state.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the connection-state advantage of stateful firewalls.

questions.question: A static packet-filtering firewall makes allow/deny decisions based on:

options.label: A
options.text: Source/destination IP addresses, protocols, and port numbers

options.label: D
options.text: The physical temperature of the device

explanation.why_correct: A static (stateless) packet filter operates at Layer 3 and filters on IPs, protocols, and ports without tracking connection state.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Deep application-payload inspection is done by application-level gateways/NGFWs.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Biometrics are an authentication factor, not a packet-filter criterion.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Device temperature is irrelevant to filtering.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of stateless packet-filter criteria.

questions.question: An application-level gateway (proxy firewall) provides stronger content filtering than a packet filter because it:

options.label: B
options.text: Operates faster with no performance impact

options.label: C
options.text: Inspects and manages application-layer (Layer 7) data, not just headers

explanation.why_correct: An application-level gateway operates at Layer 7, inspecting and filtering application data for detailed content control (at some performance cost).

why_others_are_wrong.D: MAC-only inspection is a Layer 2 concern, not an application gateway.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Deeper inspection typically reduces performance, not improves it.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Inspecting application data is precisely its purpose.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests Layer 7 inspection by application-level gateways.

questions.question: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) typically adds which capabilities beyond traditional firewalls?

options.label: C
options.text: Deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention, and application awareness

explanation.why_correct: NGFWs combine traditional filtering with deep packet inspection, integrated IPS, application awareness, and threat intelligence.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Stateless port filtering is the most basic firewall capability, not an NGFW addition.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Media sanitization is a data-destruction activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests NGFW advanced capabilities.

questions.question: Match each firewall type (1-4) to its description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Filters on IP/protocol/port with no state (Layer 3)

options.label: B
options.text: Adds IPS, deep packet inspection, and application awareness

options.label: D
options.text: Inspects application-layer (Layer 7) content as a proxy

explanation.why_correct: Static packet filter → stateless L3 (B); Stateful inspection → tracks state L3-4 (A); Application-level gateway → L7 proxy (D); NGFW → IPS/DPI/app-aware (C).

questions.question: A company wants to host public web servers while keeping its internal network isolated, using two firewalls to create a buffer zone. This architecture is a:

options.label: B
options.text: Single bastion host with no firewall

questions.question: A bastion host is:

options.text: A backup generator for the firewall

options.text: A wireless access point for guests

options.label: D

questions.question: A company is building a site-to-site VPN across the internet and wants the ENTIRE original IP packet (header and payload) protected. Which IPsec mode should it use?

options.text: Tunnel mode (encrypts the full packet, including the original header)

options.label: B
options.text: Transport mode (encrypts only the payload, leaving the header exposed)

explanation.why_correct: IPsec tunnel mode encrypts the entire original packet (header + payload) and is typical for site-to-site/gateway VPNs; transport mode protects only the payload.

questions.question: Which IPsec component provides CONFIDENTIALITY (encryption) of the data, in addition to integrity and authentication?

questions.question: In IPsec, a Security Association (SA) defines:

questions.question: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) primarily provides:

options.label: A
options.text: A secure, encrypted tunnel for data across an untrusted network

options.label: C
options.text: Physical fire suppression in the data center

explanation.why_correct: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel (e.g., via IPsec or TLS) so data can traverse untrusted networks (like the internet) securely.

questions.question: L2TP is often paired with IPsec for VPNs because L2TP by itself:

options.label: A

options.text: Provides tunneling but no encryption, so IPsec adds the confidentiality

options.text: Encrypts data too strongly to be practical

questions.question: Network Access Control (NAC) primarily enforces security by:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypting data at rest on file servers

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing the need for any authentication

options.label: C
options.text: Checking a device's posture/compliance before (and during) granting it network access

options.label: D
options.text: Assigning public IP addresses to all devices

explanation.why_correct: NAC assesses device identity and posture (e.g., patch level, configuration) before admitting it, and can monitor compliance afterward, quarantining non-compliant devices.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Data-at-rest encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: NAC controls access; it is not a public IP assignment service.
why_others_are_wrong.B: NAC complements authentication; it does not eliminate it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the posture/compliance-checking purpose of NAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Network Access Control

questions.question: A laptop fails its health check (missing patches) when it connects. The NAC system places it on a restricted remediation network until it updates. Which NAC concepts are demonstrated?

options.label: B
options.text: Post-admission control that ignores device health

options.label: D
options.text: Pre-admission control with a quarantine/remediation network

explanation.why_correct: Pre-admission NAC evaluates device posture before granting full access; non-compliant devices are sent to a quarantine/remediation network to be fixed.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Ignoring device health contradicts the health-check described.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Agentless DNS resolution is unrelated to posture-based quarantine.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Static NAT is an address-translation method, not NAC posture control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps health-check + quarantine to pre-admission NAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Types of NAC Implementations

questions.question: IEEE 802.1X is used to provide:

options.label: A
options.text: A method to assign multicast addresses

options.label: B
options.text: A fire suppression standard for data centers

options.label: D
options.text: Port-based network access control requiring authentication before a device is allowed on the network

explanation.why_correct: 802.1X provides port-based network access control, requiring a device/user to authenticate (often via RADIUS) before the switch port or WLAN grants access.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression standards are unrelated to 802.1X.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Cable categories (Cat5/6) are unrelated to 802.1X.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Multicast addressing is Class D IP, not 802.1X.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps port-based authenticated access to 802.1X.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Network Access Control

questions.question: Which approach BEST provides confidentiality and integrity for email message content?

options.label: A
options.text: Sending email over plain SMTP with no protections

options.label: C
options.text: End-to-end message encryption/signing (e.g., S/MIME or PGP)

explanation.why_correct: S/MIME or PGP provide message-level encryption and digital signatures, protecting confidentiality and integrity (and enabling sender authentication).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Plain SMTP transmits messages in cleartext without protection.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling spam filters weakens, not strengthens, email security.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A display name does not secure message content.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps email content protection to S/MIME/PGP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Email Security

questions.question: Because VoIP carries voice over the IP network, a key security consideration is that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Requires a separate copper telephone line per call

options.label: B
options.text: Inherits IP network threats (e.g., eavesdropping, DoS) and should be segmented/encrypted

options.label: C
options.text: Is immune to network attacks because it carries voice

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be encrypted under any circumstances

explanation.why_correct: VoIP runs over IP and is exposed to network threats like eavesdropping and DoS; segmentation (e.g., voice VLANs) and encryption help protect it.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Carrying voice does not exempt VoIP from IP-based attacks.
why_others_are_wrong.D: VoIP can be encrypted (e.g., SRTP/TLS).
why_others_are_wrong.A: VoIP uses the existing IP infrastructure, not a copper line per call.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests VoIP inheriting IP network risks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Voice Communications

questions.question: Which TWO protocols provide built-in encryption/security for their function? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: SSH (secure remote access) and HTTPS (TLS-encrypted web) provide built-in security; Telnet and FTP transmit data in cleartext.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Telnet is an unencrypted remote-access protocol.
why_others_are_wrong.A: FTP transmits files and credentials in cleartext.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates secure protocols from cleartext ones.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Communication Protocols

questions.question: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) differs from a traditional network firewall in that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Inspects and filters HTTP/HTTPS application traffic to protect web apps (e.g., from injection/XSS)

options.label: B
options.text: Provides backup power to web servers

options.label: D
options.text: Only filters based on MAC addresses

explanation.why_correct: A WAF focuses on application-layer web traffic, protecting web applications from attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

why_others_are_wrong.D: MAC filtering is a Layer 2 control, not a WAF function.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Inter-AS routing is a BGP/router function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps web-app-layer protection to a WAF.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Deployment Strategies

questions.question: The IPsec Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, but notably does NOT provide:

explanation.why_correct: AH provides integrity, authentication, non-repudiation, and anti-replay, but it does not encrypt the data (no confidentiality)—ESP is needed for that.

why_others_are_wrong.D: AH does help protect against replay attacks.
why_others_are_wrong.B: AH does provide data integrity.
why_others_are_wrong.C: AH does provide source authentication.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests that AH lacks confidentiality (no encryption).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Components of IPsec

questions.question: Which TWO are NAC deployment models described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: NAC can be deployed agent-based (software on the endpoint) or agentless (no installed agent); these are the two models described.

why_others_are_wrong.C: "Tunnel-mode" is an IPsec mode, not a NAC deployment model.
why_others_are_wrong.A: "Multicast NAC" is not a defined NAC deployment model.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the agent-based vs agentless NAC models.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Deployment Models

questions.question: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used to:

options.label: B
options.text: Assign dynamic IP addresses to clients

options.label: C
options.text: Resolve a domain name to an IP address

options.label: D
options.text: Resolve a known IP address to its corresponding MAC address

explanation.why_correct: ARP maps a known IP (Layer 3) address to a MAC (Layer 2) address for local frame delivery.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Name-to-IP resolution is DNS.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Web traffic encryption is TLS/HTTPS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Dynamic IP assignment is DHCP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps IP-to-MAC resolution to ARP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Layer 2 - Data Link Layer Protocols

questions.question: In network defense, firewalls are commonly described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A backup power source for the network

options.label: B
options.text: A first line of defense that controls traffic between trust zones

options.label: C
options.text: A method of physically destroying data

options.label: D
options.text: A protocol for resolving domain names

explanation.why_correct: Firewalls form a first line of network defense, enforcing policy on traffic between zones of differing trust.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Data destruction is sanitization, not a firewall.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Name resolution is DNS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of firewalls as a first line of network defense.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Firewalls Concepts

questions.question: To strengthen remote-access security for a VPN, the BEST practice among these is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Share a single VPN password across all employees

options.label: B
options.text: Allow any device to connect without checks

options.label: C
options.text: Require multi-factor authentication for remote users

explanation.why_correct: Requiring MFA significantly reduces the risk of compromised remote-access credentials being used by attackers.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Allowing unchecked devices invites compromised endpoints onto the network.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Shared passwords destroy accountability and are easily leaked.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Disabling logging removes visibility and forensic capability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps strong remote-access security to MFA.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Objective 4.3

questions.question: A multi-homed firewall is characterized by:

options.label: B
options.text: Being unable to enforce any policy

options.label: C
options.text: Operating only at the physical layer

options.label: D
options.text: Having multiple network interfaces connecting different network segments/zones

explanation.why_correct: A multi-homed firewall has two or more network interfaces, each connected to a different segment/zone, allowing it to control traffic between them.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A single interface would be single-homed, not multi-homed.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Multi-homed firewalls do enforce policy between their interfaces.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Firewalls operate at Layers 3-7, not only the physical layer.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the multi-interface multi-homed firewall.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Firewall Architecture

questions.question: The Domain Name System (DNS) primarily:

options.label: C
options.text: Resolves human-readable domain names to IP addresses

options.label: D
options.text: Assigns MAC addresses to network cards

explanation.why_correct: DNS translates domain names (e.g., example.com) into IP addresses so traffic can be routed.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Email encryption is handled by S/MIME/PGP/TLS, not DNS.
why_others_are_wrong.D: MAC addresses are hardware-assigned, not by DNS.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of DNS name resolution.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Networking Concepts > Layer 7 - Application Layer Protocols

questions.question: A screened-host architecture combines a packet-filtering router with:

options.label: A
options.text: A bastion host that the router directs external traffic to

options.label: B
options.text: A wireless mesh of access points

explanation.why_correct: A screened host uses a screening router plus a bastion host; the router filters traffic and directs permitted external traffic to the hardened bastion host.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Dual internet connections describe redundancy, not the screened-host design.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A wireless mesh is a topology, not this firewall architecture.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A degausser destroys data; it is unrelated to firewall architecture.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the router + bastion host screened-host design.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Screened Host

questions.question: Gathering information about a target using publicly available sources (OSINT) without directly interacting with the target systems is:

explanation.why_correct: Passive reconnaissance collects information from public sources (OSINT) without touching the target, making it harder to detect.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Active reconnaissance directly probes the target (e.g., port scanning), which can be detected.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A DoS attack disrupts availability, not information gathering.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ARP poisoning is a spoofing attack, not reconnaissance via OSINT.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes passive (OSINT) from active reconnaissance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Reconnaissance Attacks

questions.question: An attacker runs a port scan against a company's public IP range to find open services. This activity is BEST classified as:

explanation.why_correct: Port scanning directly interacts with the target to enumerate open services, which is active reconnaissance (and is detectable by monitoring).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Passive recon uses public sources without touching the target; scanning is direct interaction.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A teardrop attack sends overlapping fragments to crash a host, not enumerate services.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A replay attack reuses captured messages, not scanning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps port scanning to active reconnaissance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Reconnaissance Attacks

questions.question: Which TWO activities are forms of reconnaissance? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: OSINT gathering (passive) and port/service scanning (active) are reconnaissance activities used to profile a target.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Reinstalling encryption keys describes a KRACK attack, not reconnaissance.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Flooding a server is a denial-of-service attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies passive and active reconnaissance forms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Reconnaissance Attacks

questions.question: On a LAN, an attacker sends forged ARP replies so that traffic destined for the gateway is instead sent to the attacker's machine, enabling interception. This attack is:

explanation.why_correct: ARP poisoning sends forged ARP replies that map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC, letting the attacker intercept traffic (man-in-the-middle) on the local segment.

why_others_are_wrong.A: DNS poisoning corrupts name resolution, not ARP/MAC mappings on the LAN.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A Smurf attack is an ICMP amplification DoS, not interception.
why_others_are_wrong.C: War driving is searching for wireless networks while moving.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps forged-ARP interception to ARP poisoning/MITM.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Key Attack Methods

questions.question: An attacker alters DNS records so users typing a legitimate bank URL are redirected to a malicious look-alike site. This is DNS poisoning, and the BEST defense is:

options.label: D
options.text: Using a hub instead of a switch

explanation.why_correct: DNS poisoning redirects traffic via forged DNS data; DNSSEC adds cryptographic authentication of DNS responses to detect/prevent tampering.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling logging reduces visibility and does not defend DNS integrity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A hub worsens security and does not protect DNS.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A taller fence is a physical control unrelated to DNS poisoning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps DNS poisoning defense to DNSSEC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Key Attack Methods

questions.question: IP spoofing involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Changing a device's MAC address to bypass filtering

options.label: B
options.text: Flooding a target with ICMP echo replies

options.label: C
options.text: Forging the source IP address in packet headers to appear as a trusted source

options.label: D
options.text: Redirecting DNS lookups to malicious servers

explanation.why_correct: IP spoofing manipulates the source IP in packet headers to impersonate a trusted host and bypass IP-based controls.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Changing a MAC address is MAC spoofing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Redirecting DNS lookups is DNS spoofing/poisoning.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Flooding with ICMP replies relates to a Smurf/amplification DoS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes IP spoofing from MAC/DNS spoofing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Key Attack Methods

questions.question: Which control helps defend against MAC spoofing at the data link layer by restricting which devices may use a switch port?

explanation.why_correct: Port security/MAC filtering restricts switch ports to authorized MAC addresses, reducing the risk of spoofing at Layer 2.

why_others_are_wrong.D: DNSSEC protects DNS responses, not switch-port MAC access.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A generator provides power, not MAC access control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A sprinkler is a fire-suppression control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps Layer 2 spoofing defense to port security/MAC filtering.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Defensive Measures

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are spoofing/poisoning attacks? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: ARP poisoning and DNS spoofing falsify mappings/records to redirect or intercept traffic.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A teardrop attack is a DoS using overlapping fragments, not spoofing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: War chalking is marking locations of wireless networks, not spoofing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies spoofing/poisoning attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Key Attack Methods

questions.question: A Smurf attack amplifies traffic against a victim by:

options.label: B
options.text: Sending oversized packets that exceed the MTU

options.label: D
options.text: Spoofing the victim's IP and broadcasting ICMP echo requests so many hosts reply to the victim

explanation.why_correct: A Smurf attack spoofs the victim's source IP and sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address; all responders flood the victim with replies (amplification).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Oversized packets exceeding MTU describe a Ping of Death.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Reinstalling WPA2 keys describes KRACK.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Marking locations is war chalking.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps ICMP broadcast amplification to the Smurf attack.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Reflection and Amplification Attacks

questions.question: A Fraggle attack is similar to a Smurf attack but uses which protocol for its echo flood?

explanation.why_correct: A Fraggle attack is the UDP-echo analog of the Smurf attack (which uses ICMP echo).

why_others_are_wrong.C: ICMP echo is used by the Smurf attack.
why_others_are_wrong.D: TCP is not the protocol used in a Fraggle attack.
why_others_are_wrong.B: ARP is not used for the Fraggle echo flood.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes Fraggle (UDP) from Smurf (ICMP).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Reflection and Amplification Attacks

questions.question: A Ping of Death attack crashes vulnerable systems by:

options.label: B
options.text: Sending malformed or oversized packets that exceed the maximum allowed size (MTU)

options.label: D
options.text: Spoofing ARP replies on the LAN

explanation.why_correct: A Ping of Death sends oversized/malformed packets exceeding the MTU that some systems mishandle, causing crashes.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Forging ARP replies is ARP poisoning.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Cracking WPA2 handshakes relates to KRACK/wireless attacks.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Forging DNS records is DNS poisoning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps oversized-packet crashes to Ping of Death.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Legacy Attacks

questions.question: A Land attack causes a target to malfunction by sending SYN packets where:

options.label: A
options.text: The DNS record points to a malicious site

options.label: B
options.text: The ARP table is flooded with random MACs

options.label: C
options.text: The payload is encrypted with the target's public key

options.label: D
options.text: The source and destination IP are both set to the target's own address

explanation.why_correct: A Land attack spoofs SYN packets with the target's own IP as both source and destination, causing the machine to attempt to connect to itself and hang/crash.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Encryption with a public key is not how a Land attack works.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Pointing DNS to a malicious site is DNS poisoning.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Flooding the ARP table is a different (CAM/ARP) attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps the self-addressed SYN to a Land attack.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Legacy Attacks

questions.question: A Teardrop attack crashes a system by sending:

options.label: D
options.text: Fragmented packets with overlapping payloads that fail during reassembly

explanation.why_correct: A Teardrop attack sends overlapping/malformed IP fragments that crash systems unable to correctly reassemble them.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A single oversized ping is the Ping of Death.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Forged ARP replies are ARP poisoning.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Unsolicited Bluetooth messages are bluejacking.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps overlapping-fragment crashes to Teardrop.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Network Security and Attacks > Legacy Attacks

questions.question: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack differs from a basic DoS attack in that a DDoS:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypts the victim's files for ransom

options.label: B
options.text: Relies on a single host with a slow connection

options.label: D
options.text: Uses many compromised systems (a botnet) to flood the target simultaneously

explanation.why_correct: A DDoS leverages many distributed, often compromised hosts (a botnet) to overwhelm the target, making it harder to block than a single-source DoS.

why_others_are_wrong.C: DDoS can target any network service, not only wireless.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Encrypting files for ransom is ransomware, not DDoS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A single slow host describes a limited DoS, not a distributed attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes distributed (botnet) DDoS from single-source DoS.

questions.question: Which TWO strategies help mitigate denial-of-service attacks? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Rate limiting/traffic analysis and load balancing/redundancy help absorb and detect DoS traffic, reducing impact on any single point.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling firewalls removes a key filtering defense.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Sharing admin passwords harms security and does not mitigate DoS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound DoS mitigations.

questions.question: Match each network attack (1-4) to its description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Forges ARP replies to intercept LAN traffic (MITM)

options.label: B
options.text: Alters DNS records to redirect users to malicious sites

options.label: C
options.text: Sends SYN packets with the target's IP as both source and destination

options.label: D
options.text: Spoofs the victim IP and floods it via ICMP broadcast replies
