questions.question: Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) is considered insecure largely because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Requires multi-factor authentication for every packet

options.label: B
options.text: Uses 256-bit AES with strong key management

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be used on any wireless network

options.label: D
options.text: Uses the weak RC4 cipher with flawed key handling

explanation.why_correct: WEP relies on the RC4 stream cipher with weak IV/key handling, making it easily cracked; it should be replaced by WPA2/WPA3.

why_others_are_wrong.A: WEP does not use per-packet MFA.
why_others_are_wrong.C: WEP can technically run on wireless networks but is insecure.

questions.question: WPA2 improved wireless security over WPA primarily by introducing:

explanation.why_correct: WPA2 uses CCMP (based on AES), providing stronger encryption than WPA's TKIP and WEP's RC4.

why_others_are_wrong.B: RC4 is the weak cipher used by WEP.
why_others_are_wrong.C: WPA2 encrypts traffic; it is not cleartext.
why_others_are_wrong.A: WPS is a convenience feature with security weaknesses, not WPA2's core improvement.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps WPA2 to CCMP/AES.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Encryption Protocols

questions.question: WPA3 strengthens key exchange against offline password-guessing attacks by using:

explanation.why_correct: WPA3 introduces SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) for a more secure handshake that resists offline dictionary attacks, plus stronger AES key sizes.

why_others_are_wrong.A: RC4 is the weak WEP cipher.
why_others_are_wrong.C: WEP shared keys are insecure and not used by WPA3.
why_others_are_wrong.D: WPA3 does not exchange the PSK in cleartext.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps WPA3 secure key exchange to SAE.

questions.question: Which TWO wireless security protocols are considered STRONG/current choices (versus deprecated ones)? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: WPA2 (CCMP/AES) and WPA3 (SAE/AES) are the strong, current choices; WEP and open networks are insecure/deprecated.

why_others_are_wrong.D: WEP is deprecated and easily broken.
why_others_are_wrong.C: An open network provides no encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates strong wireless encryption from deprecated options.

questions.question: Why is Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) generally NOT recommended?

options.text: Its PIN-based setup is vulnerable to brute-force attacks

questions.question: At an airport, an attacker sets up a rogue access point named "Airport_Free_WiFi" that mimics the legitimate network to capture victims' credentials. This is BEST described as:

questions.question: An employee plugs an unauthorized wireless access point into the corporate LAN to get better Wi-Fi at their desk. The security concern is that this is a:

options.label: A
options.text: Rogue access point that bypasses network security controls

explanation.why_correct: A rogue access point is an unauthorized AP connected to the network that bypasses security controls and creates an uncontrolled entry point.

why_others_are_wrong.C: DNSSEC authenticates DNS responses; it is unrelated.
why_others_are_wrong.B: 802.1X is port-based access control, not an unauthorized AP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps an unauthorized AP to a rogue access point.

questions.question: A Key Reinstallation Attack (KRACK) exploits a weakness in:

options.label: B
options.text: The WPA2 four-way handshake, forcing reuse of encryption keys

options.label: C
options.text: The ARP cache on a switch

explanation.why_correct: KRACK manipulates the WPA2 four-way handshake to force nonce/key reinstallation, enabling decryption/replay of wireless traffic.

why_others_are_wrong.A: DNS resolution is targeted by DNS poisoning, not KRACK.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ARP cache manipulation is ARP poisoning.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The TCP handshake is unrelated to WPA2 key reinstallation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps KRACK to the WPA2 handshake.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Key Wireless Network Attacks

questions.question: Driving around an area with a device to locate and identify vulnerable wireless networks is called:

explanation.why_correct: War driving is moving through an area to discover and map wireless networks (often to find vulnerable ones).

why_others_are_wrong.D: War chalking marks the discovered networks' locations.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Bluejacking sends unsolicited Bluetooth messages.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Bluesnarfing steals data over Bluetooth.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of war driving.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Key Wireless Network Attacks

questions.question: Marking physical locations with symbols to indicate the presence of open or vulnerable wireless networks is:

explanation.why_correct: War chalking uses symbols/markings to advertise the location and characteristics of nearby wireless networks for others to exploit.

why_others_are_wrong.C: War driving is the act of moving around to find networks.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Signal jamming is a wireless DoS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: An evil twin is an impostor access point.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of war chalking.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Key Wireless Network Attacks

questions.question: Wireless signal jamming is a form of which attack category?

explanation.why_correct: Signal jamming floods the radio frequency to disrupt wireless communications—a denial-of-service attack on availability.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Spoofing falsifies identity/records, not RF disruption.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Reconnaissance gathers information rather than disrupting service.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Privilege escalation gains higher access, not RF disruption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Classifies jamming as a wireless DoS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Key Wireless Network Attacks

questions.question: Forcing a Bluetooth connection to access and steal stored data from a device is known as:

explanation.why_correct: Bluesnarfing forces a Bluetooth connection to access/steal data stored on the target device.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Bluejacking sends unsolicited messages, not data theft.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Bluebugging takes control of the device to execute commands.
why_others_are_wrong.D: War driving is wireless-network discovery.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes bluesnarfing (data theft) from other Bluetooth attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Bluetooth Security Threats

questions.question: Gaining control of a device over Bluetooth to execute commands without the user's knowledge is:

explanation.why_correct: Bluebugging gives an attacker control of a device to execute commands covertly over Bluetooth.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Bluejacking only sends unsolicited messages.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Bluesnarfing steals stored data but does not necessarily control the device.
why_others_are_wrong.A: War chalking marks wireless network locations.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps covert device control to bluebugging.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 4 > Wireless Networking Introduction > Bluetooth Security Threats

questions.question: Which TWO are Bluetooth-specific security threats? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Bluejacking (unsolicited messages) and bluesnarfing (data theft) are Bluetooth-specific attacks.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A Smurf attack is an ICMP amplification DoS on IP networks.
why_others_are_wrong.B: DNS poisoning targets name resolution, not Bluetooth.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies Bluetooth-specific attacks.

questions.question: The BSSID in a wireless network refers to:

options.label: B
options.text: The encryption key used by clients

options.label: C
options.text: The MAC address of a specific access point

options.label: D
options.text: The IP address of the default gateway

explanation.why_correct: The BSSID (Basic SSID) is the MAC address of a specific access point; the ESSID is the network name shared across multiple APs.

why_others_are_wrong.A: The network name is the SSID/ESSID, not the BSSID.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The encryption key is separate from the BSSID.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The gateway IP is unrelated to the BSSID.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes BSSID (AP MAC) from ESSID (network name).

questions.question: In wireless infrastructure mode, client devices communicate:

options.label: A
options.text: Only directly device-to-device with no access point

options.label: C
options.text: Through a central access point rather than directly peer-to-peer

explanation.why_correct: Infrastructure mode routes client traffic through a central access point; ad-hoc mode is the peer-to-peer alternative with no AP.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Direct device-to-device with no AP describes ad-hoc mode.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Wireless uses radio, not fiber cabling.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Wireless inherently uses radio frequencies.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes infrastructure (AP-based) from ad-hoc mode.

questions.question: An employee's smartphone containing corporate data is lost. Which MDM control BEST protects the data on that device?

options.label: A
options.text: Disabling the company VPN for everyone

options.label: B
options.text: Removing the screen lock to ease recovery

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the office Wi-Fi signal strength

options.label: D
options.text: Remote device sanitization (remote wipe), ideally combined with device encryption

explanation.why_correct: MDM remote wipe lets administrators sanitize a lost/stolen device remotely; with data-at-rest encryption, the data is protected even before the wipe completes.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Disabling the VPN does not protect data already on the lost device.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wi-Fi signal strength is irrelevant to protecting a lost device.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Removing the screen lock weakens protection of the device.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps protecting a lost device to MDM remote wipe + encryption.

questions.question: An MDM "geofencing" control enforces security policies based on:

options.label: A
options.text: The color of the device case

options.label: B
options.text: The physical location of the device

options.label: C
options.text: The brand of the device charger

explanation.why_correct: Geofencing applies location-based access and permissions, e.g., restricting features when a device leaves an approved area.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Case color is irrelevant to geofencing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: App count is not the basis of geofencing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Charger brand is irrelevant.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps location-based MDM policy to geofencing.

questions.question: Which TWO are MDM controls that protect enterprise mobile devices? (Select TWO.)

options.label: D
options.text: Enforcing encryption for data at rest

explanation.why_correct: Encryption of data at rest and inactivity/session timeouts are MDM controls that reduce data exposure on mobile devices.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling passcodes weakens device security.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Allowing untrusted apps increases malware risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies protective MDM controls.

questions.question: Which is a recommended general measure to harden a wireless network?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the factory default admin password

options.label: B
options.text: Broadcast the admin credentials in the SSID

options.label: C
options.text: Change default passwords/SSIDs and use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the network open to maximize compatibility

explanation.why_correct: Changing default credentials/SSIDs and using strong encryption (WPA2/WPA3) are core wireless hardening steps, ideally with a defense-in-depth approach.

why_others_are_wrong.D: An open network exposes traffic to anyone in range.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Default admin passwords are widely known and easily abused.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Broadcasting credentials in the SSID exposes them to attackers.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound wireless hardening practices.

questions.question: What primarily distinguishes an evil twin from a generic rogue access point?

options.label: A
options.text: A rogue AP always uses WPA3 encryption

options.label: B
options.text: An evil twin is always authorized by IT

options.label: C
options.text: An evil twin only affects wired networks

options.label: D
options.text: An evil twin deliberately impersonates a legitimate SSID to deceive users into connecting

explanation.why_correct: An evil twin is a rogue AP specifically configured to mimic a legitimate network's SSID to trick users; a generic rogue AP is simply an unauthorized AP, not necessarily impersonating one.

why_others_are_wrong.B: An evil twin is malicious and unauthorized, not IT-sanctioned.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A rogue AP's encryption is attacker-chosen and often weak/open, not guaranteed WPA3.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Evil twins target wireless clients, not wired-only networks.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the impersonation distinction of an evil twin.

questions.question: Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) improves wireless throughput by:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminating the need for any access point

options.label: B
options.text: Sending all data on a single narrow frequency

options.label: D
options.text: Dividing data into multiple substreams sent over separate subchannels

explanation.why_correct: OFDM splits data into multiple substreams across separate orthogonal subchannels, increasing throughput and resilience to interference.

why_others_are_wrong.B: OFDM uses multiple subchannels, not a single narrow frequency.
why_others_are_wrong.C: OFDM is a modulation/multiplexing method, not an encryption cipher.
why_others_are_wrong.A: OFDM does not remove the need for an access point.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of OFDM multi-subchannel operation.
